title: After the Clarity Act Stalled, US Regulators Are Writing Crypto Rules Themselves
excerpt: Days after the Senate's 49-50 vote, the SEC opened a path for tokenized stocks and the CFTC sent a crypto rule to the White House.
body:
• The Senate blocked the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on a 49-50 procedural vote September 15, eleven short of the 60 needed.
  • Within 48 hours, the SEC issued a five-year exemption for trading tokenized US stocks and the CFTC sent a crypto rule to White House review.
  • SEC Chair Paul Atkins says the agency's crypto agenda will continue "with or without" legislation.

The US Senate failed on September 15 to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, the comprehensive crypto market-structure bill known as H.R. 3633. The 49-50 procedural vote fell 11 short of the 60 needed for cloture. But crypto rulemaking didn't stop — it relocated from Capitol Hill to the federal regulators, and it moved fast.

The vote

All 49 yes votes came from Republicans. Four Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Jerry Moran and Thom Tillis — voted no, and no Democrat voted yes. Tillis first voted yes, then switched, preserving the right to move for reconsideration. The House had passed the same bill 294-134 in July 2025. Negotiations collapsed over ethics provisions tied to President Trump's crypto interests, anti-money-laundering safeguards, and bank warnings that stablecoin rewards could drain deposits from traditional lenders.

The regulators move in

On September 17, two days after the vote, the SEC issued a five-year innovation exemption creating a temporary path for trading tokenized US stocks — inching financial markets toward 24/7 trading. The same day, the CFTC sent a crypto markets rule to the White House for review at the prerule stage, and issued a no-action letter giving relief to passive software providers.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins, speaking at the Solana Policy Institute, backed the bill but added the agency's agenda would continue regardless of Congress. CFTC Chair Michael Selig had already directed staff in August to prepare crypto market rules in case congressional negotiations failed.

"With or without that legislation, this Administration will deliver for American investors and technological innovators."

— Paul Atkins, Chair, Securities and Exchange Commission

Industry reaction

The industry, which spent heavily lobbying for the bill, is pivoting to the agencies. "At this point, I don't think we can wait any longer for Congress and the Senate," Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong told CNBC after the vote. Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott urged agencies to produce "clear rules of the road" until Congress legislates.

Blockchain Association CEO Summer Mersinger, a former CFTC commissioner, said regulatory uncertainty is blocking traditional finance from entering: "Having the regulators provide some sort of certainty is going to really open up the industry to more investment." Former CFTC Chair J. Christopher Giancarlo told journalist Eleanor Terrett that Atkins and Selig are "determined to do what their jobs require them to do and put in place sound regulatory frameworks." Bernstein analysts led by Gautam Chhugani expect swift agency action on token classification, DeFi and self-custody protections, and equity tokenization.

What stays the same — for now

With the bill stalled, the stablecoin rewards framework is unchanged, so platforms like Coinbase can keep offering rewards on idle balances. Prediction markets have cratered on revival hopes: Polymarket odds of passage in 2026 fell from 82 percent to 16 percent. Fintech attorney Felix Shipkevich told TechTarget he "would not be surprised if we have to wait until after elections" for another vote.

The India angle

India's diaspora includes some of crypto's biggest founders and investors, and the US rulebook shapes where they build. A regime written by regulators rather than Congress also matters in New Delhi, where policymakers have kept crypto in a holding pattern — 30 percent taxation, FIU registration — while watching Washington. Agency-led rules tend to be narrower and more reversible than statutes, which cuts both ways for builders choosing jurisdictions.

What's next

Watch the White House review of the CFTC rule, the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption rollout, and whether Tillis files his motion to reconsider — the bill's only remaining procedural lifeline.
